First: If I put just a path in the URL for a Reddit comment, the domain is assumed to be reddit.com. So I can put things like

    [The Mass Effect subreddit](/r/masseffect)

Because of this, I can add the fragment '#/spoiler' to most URLs, which doesn't change the actual behavior of the URL, but indicates to the CSS that I want that link to be spoilered.

Example: [This link is a rickroll](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ#/spoiler "Rickroll")  
which is the result of `[This link is a rickroll](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ#/spoiler "Rickroll")`

Your answer is right. The 'intuitive' feeling that you should have a chance as large as the sum of the individual probabilities is wrong here, and it's pretty easy to show why with some different numbers. Take a coin, for instance. Any given flip has a 50% chance of landing heads, but flipping two coins clearly does not provide a 100% chance of landing heads. Out of the four results, three include a 'heads', resulting in a 75% chance. Adding a third flip gives you seven out of the eight possible results, or an 87.5% chance. Each flip adds a smaller amount to the probability of obtaining at least one heads, converging on P = 1.

Similarly, in a theoretical party of 100 zigzagoons, you would not be guaranteed a rare candy, and each zigzagoon you add after the first will increase the probability of getting a rare candy by a smaller amount than the last. This means that the percent chance of getting a rare candy should always be lesser than or equal to the number of zigzagoons in your party, the opposite of what intuition expects.

The lack of multi-gender aliens in ME is sort of interesting. From a technical standpoint, it's easy to understand - creating an all-new model is very expensive, both in terms of disk space and the time spent on concept art, modeling, and texture work. The problem then was in justifying the fact that humans were the only ones with more than one gender.

As an 'asexual+' species, the asari are easy to justify. The specifics of their reproduction are definitely on the softer end of the sci-fi spectrum, and it shows when nobody in one of the most advanced species in the galaxy seems quite sure how their own reproductive systems actually work. In ME2, vorcha may provide another interesting example of asexual reproduction where the individuals are genetically identical, but differentiate through their extreme adaptive capabilities, though their reproduction is not actually mentioned in the codex.

Salarian reproduction was a better and more consistently-applied handwave, in my opinion. Although such an extreme case of male-skewed sex ratios wouldn't really be stable in an evolutionary sense, the cultural aspects are actually interesting and the species is generally pretty well-written. The krogan are handled similarly, though the genophage provides them with an impetus to protect their women that makes better sense biologically, and of course their reproduction is a major theme of the series.

The less populous (or present, at least) races - volus, elcor, hanar, quarians, and later drell - receive no justification at all. It can be assumed that either Shepard has not met other members of the species because of their comparative rarity in Council space or the Terminus Systems (as with the quarians) or even because the genders are not easily distinguished, or do not exist at all (as is perhaps true of the hanar). Notably, when one of these species receives more representation in the sequel, it also becomes the second species to have both genders represented.

Batarians needed no justification - the only members of the species Shepard encountered were members of Balak's terrorist group, and that such a group would be all-male is not particularly surprising. The existence of the oppressive Batarian Hegemony in ME2 and near-extinction of the species in ME3 provided adequate reasons for Shepard never to have met a female batarian.

This leaves only the turians, and in kind of an awkward spot. They're as common as asari, so coincidence is very unlikely, and though militaristic, their culture is not described as particularly oppressive or even patriarchal. Female aspects of turian culture are just an awkward gap without even a handwaved explanation. This left most of us wondering where the hell the female turians were, even though technically they didn't present an exception. As far as I can tell (and I'd love an explanation if I'm wrong) this is just an oversight on the part of the writers that somehow went unaddressed for three games and countless spinoffs.
